hints: Check your formula against the two limits: a flat prior and a very tight one.
behaviours.spec: `post.mean` equals `A \ (X'y / sigma^2)` up to rounding (relative error about cond(A) times eps); it tends to the least-squares fit as `tau` grows and to zero as `tau` shrinks.
test_hints: Compare with the formula, computed in the test in a different way (for example with an explicit inverse), with a tolerance from cond(A).

hints: The covariance is the inverse of the precision, not the precision itself.
behaviours.spec: `post.cov` is symmetric (exactly), positive definite, and `post.cov * A` equals the identity within a tolerance derived from cond(A).
test_hints: Test the properties a covariance must have, then its value.

hints: The formula squares `sigma` and `tau`, so a negative value gives a plausible answer for a meaningless input.
behaviours.spec: A `y` whose length differs from the number of rows of `X` throws a `DimensionMismatch`; `sigma <= 0` or `tau <= 0` throws an `ArgumentError`.

milestones.goal:
The conjugate posterior in closed form. Form the precision `A`, then get the
mean by solving a linear system with it and the covariance from a
factorisation of it (`A` is symmetric positive definite, so a Cholesky
factorisation exists). Tests compare with the formula and with its two
limits: a very wide prior (the posterior mean becomes the least-squares fit)
and a very tight one (it shrinks to zero).

choices: It moves towards the least-squares fit `X \ y`
It moves towards zero
It stays the same: the prior does not affect the mean
It becomes undefined, because the prior has no variance left
questions.explain: The prior's precision `I / tau^2` goes to zero, so `A` becomes `X'X / sigma^2` and the mean becomes the solution of the normal equations, the least-squares fit.
misconceptions: That is the other limit: a tiny `tau` (a tight prior around zero) pulls the mean to zero.
The prior adds `I / tau^2` to the precision; for small or moderate `tau` it shrinks the mean towards zero.
A large `tau` is a wide prior, a large variance; it is a small `tau` that leaves little variance.
questions.prompt: With 20 rows of data, what happens to the posterior mean as `tau` grows from 1 to 1e6?

api.doc: Coefficients `w ~ MvNormal(zeros(k), tau^2 I)`, observations `y ~ MvNormal(X w, sigma^2 I)`, with `y` observed.

hints: Evaluate the prior part of the model at a fixed `w` and compare with the formula by hand.
behaviours.spec: `logprior(model, (w = w,))` equals the log density of `N(0, tau^2 I)` at `w`, `-k/2 log(2 pi tau^2) - |w|^2 / (2 tau^2)`, up to rounding.
test_hints: Compare `logprior` with the formula written out by hand.

hints: Evaluate the likelihood part at a fixed `w` and compare with the formula by hand.
behaviours.spec: `loglikelihood(model, (w = w,))` equals `-n/2 log(2 pi sigma^2) - |y - X w|^2 / (2 sigma^2)` up to rounding, and `logjoint` is the sum of the two.
test_hints: Compare `loglikelihood` with the formula written out by hand.

milestones.goal:
Write the same model as a Turing `@model`. A model is a log density you can
evaluate before sampling anything: `logprior(model, (w = w,))`,
`loglikelihood(model, (w = w,))` and `logjoint(model, (w = w,))` evaluate it
at a given `w`. Test those against the normal log densities written out by
hand. `@model` functions take positional arguments; write the model with
positional `sigma` and `tau` and let `regression_model` pass its keywords
on (and check them as in milestone 1).

choices: about 0.71
questions.explain: The second argument of `MvNormal` is a covariance: `sigma * I` gives every observation variance 0.5, so a standard deviation of sqrt(0.5), about 0.71. The intended model needs `sigma^2 * I`.
misconceptions: That would be the case for `sigma^2 * I`; the matrix holds variances, not standard deviations.
0.25 is `sigma^2`, the variance the model was meant to have; this one has variance 0.5.
`I` alone would give variance 1; it is scaled by 0.5 here.
questions.prompt: A model has `y ~ MvNormal(X * w, sigma * I)` with `sigma = 0.5`. What noise standard deviation does it assume?

behaviours.spec: Each sampled posterior mean is within 4 Monte Carlo standard errors (posterior sd over the square root of the effective sample size) of the exact mean; for a normal sampling error that bound fails with probability about 6e-5 per coefficient, which the test states.

milestones.goal:
Sample the model with NUTS and compare with the exact posterior. Turing 0.49
returns a FlexiChains chain: `chain[@varname(w)]` holds one coefficient
vector per draw. `using Turing.FlexiChains: mcse, ess` gives the Monte Carlo
standard error and effective sample size per coefficient,
`mcse(chain)[@varname(w[1])]`. Keep `n` small in your tests (a few hundred
to 1000): every check runs them several times.

choices: About 0.11, the posterior sd
Zero: NUTS is exact for a normal posterior
questions.explain: The Monte Carlo standard error is the sd over the square root of the effective sample size. Correlated draws carry less information than independent ones: these 1000 are worth about 250.
misconceptions: That treats the draws as independent; successive NUTS draws are correlated, so the chain is worth 250 independent draws, not 1000.
The sd is the spread of the posterior itself; the error of a mean of many draws is much smaller.
NUTS draws converge to the posterior, but any finite chain's mean has Monte Carlo error.
questions.prompt: 1000 NUTS draws of a coefficient have sd 0.11 and ESS 250. How far from the exact posterior mean is their mean typically?

choices: So the test gives the same verdict on every run; the margin then says how far that one run is from failing
Because NUTS draws are independent of each other only when the sampler starts from a fixed seed, and the 6e-5 assumes independent draws
Because without a seed the MCSE cannot be computed
questions.explain: With a fixed seed a test either passes every time or fails every time on the pinned versions, so it cannot flake; the 4 MCSE margin is what makes it likely that a correct sampler passes for that seed, and the observed margin is worth stating.
misconceptions: The seed fixes which draws you get, not how they depend on each other; NUTS draws stay correlated.
MCSE comes from the draws themselves (their sd and autocorrelation); any chain has one, seeded or not.
questions.prompt: A test passes when the sampled mean is within 4 MCSE of the exact mean, with the seed fixed. Why fix the seed if 4 MCSE already fails only about 6e-5 of the time?

api.doc: Central `level` interval of the posterior predictive at `xnew` for `post = posterior_exact(...)`.
The same from an `n × k` matrix of draws of `w` (as `coefficient_draws` returns): the mean and variance of `draws * xnew`, plus the noise variance.

hints: The prediction is uncertain for two reasons; both add to its variance.
behaviours.spec: From the exact posterior: the interval is `mu ± z s` with `mu = xnew'm`, `s^2 = xnew'C xnew + sigma^2` and `z` the normal quantile at `(1 + level) / 2`, up to rounding.
test_hints: Compute the interval in the test from the formula and compare.

hints: The keyword must change the result, and nonsense values must be refused.
behaviours.spec: The keyword `level` sets the coverage (a higher level gives a wider interval); a `level` outside (0, 1) throws an `ArgumentError`.
test_hints: Call with a level other than the default and check the effect.

hints: From draws, the coefficient part of the predictive variance is the spread of `draws * xnew`.
behaviours.spec: From `n` independent draws of the exact posterior, each end of the interval is within 5 standard errors of the exact interval's end (the standard error of the mean and of the variance of `draws * xnew`, derived in the test).
test_hints: Draw independent samples from `MvNormal(post.mean, post.cov)` with a seeded `Xoshiro` and compare with the exact interval.

milestones.goal:
Predictive intervals for a new input `xnew`. A new observation is uncertain
for two reasons: the coefficients are uncertain (variance `xnew' C xnew`)
and the noise is added on top (variance `sigma^2`). Both are normal here, so
the predictive is normal and its central interval uses the normal quantile:
`quantile(Normal(), p)`. Write one method for the exact posterior and one
for a matrix of draws; test the draws version with independent draws from
`MvNormal(post.mean, post.cov)` (fast, and its Monte Carlo error is
derivable), not with NUTS.

choices: It shrinks to zero width
It shrinks towards a width set by the noise, about 2 * 1.645 * sigma
It stays the same width
It grows, because each row adds noise
questions.explain: More data shrinks the coefficient variance `xnew' C xnew` towards zero, but a new observation still carries its own noise, variance `sigma^2`; the width tends to `2 z sigma` with `z = 1.645`.
misconceptions: That is the interval for the mean `xnew'w`, not for a new observation, which has noise of its own.
The coefficient part of the variance falls as data are added; only the noise part stays.
The noise of the data is already in the posterior; more rows make the coefficients more certain, not less.
questions.prompt: With 20 rows of data, how does the 90% predictive interval at a fixed `xnew` change as more rows are added?

projects.name: bayesreg
projects.reading:
Prerequisites: course unit 27 (probabilistic programming).

The model: `y = X w + noise`, noise `N(0, sigma^2)` per row with `sigma`
known, and the prior `w ~ N(0, tau^2 I)`. Then the posterior of `w` is
normal, with precision `A = X'X / sigma^2 + I / tau^2`, covariance `inv(A)`
and mean `A \ (X'y / sigma^2)`. Milestone 1 is that formula; everything
after it is checked against it.

Keep test data tiny (20 rows, 2 coefficients) and draw it with a seeded
`Xoshiro`: sampling is the slow part of this project, and every check runs
your tests several times. Every random function takes an `rng`. Every
tolerance in your tests gets a comment saying where it comes from: the
conditioning of `A` for exact formulas, the Monte Carlo standard error for
samples. This env runs in the container only on Windows hosts.
projects.summary: Build Bayesian linear regression twice: first the exact posterior for a normal prior and known noise (closed form, tested exactly), then the same model in Turing.jl sampled with NUTS, and check that the samples agree with the exact answer within a margin derived from the effective sample size. Finish with predictive intervals from both. You write the code and the tests.

projects.name: classify
projects.reading:
Prerequisites: course unit 26 (machine learning).

`data/flowers.csv` is the file this project is about: 90 flowers of three
species (40 alba, 30 rosea, 20 viola) with four measurements each. It is
synthetic (drawn from seeded normal distributions), and one measurement,
`stem_mm`, is in millimetres while the others are in centimetres. Open it
before you start. The `ml` environment has no CSV.jl and no DataFrames.jl,
so you read the file line by line with `eachline` and `split`, and the
comparison table is a vector of named tuples.

Knet.jl is another deep-learning library for Julia, older than Flux, with
its own GPU array type and a define-by-run style close to PyTorch's. It is
not installed in this course's environments (the course covers it in text
only); the Flux part of this project is what a Knet version would replace.

Two of these libraries export functions with the same names (`fit!`,
`predict`), so load them with `import Flux`, `import MLJ`, `import BetaML`
and write qualified names (`MLJ.machine`, `BetaML.fit!`).

Randomness: every function that shuffles, initialises or samples takes an
`rng` argument, and tests pass `Xoshiro(seed)`. Julia's default stream is
stable on the pinned 1.10.13, but code that reads the global RNG cannot be
tested reproducibly. Accuracy thresholds in the acceptance tests are
calibrated on the pinned packages over a stated set of seeds, not derived;
write the same kind of comment next to every threshold in your own tests.
This project runs in the container only on Windows hosts.
projects.summary: Build the same classification task three times (a small neural network in Flux.jl, a pipeline with a decision tree in MLJ.jl, and a BetaML.jl random forest), on one seeded, stratified train/test split, and compare them in one table. You write the data handling, the training functions and the tests, including tests that do not flake.

The solver projects the state back onto S + I + R = 1 after every step

r = (sqrt(5) - 1) / 2
println(isapprox(r^2, 1 - r; rtol = 1e-15))

api.doc: use[r, p] is resource r per unit of product p. Silent solver; an `ErrorException` if the solver does not report an optimum.

hints: The optimum of a linear program sits at a vertex: list the vertices of a small case by hand and compare.
behaviours.spec: On a 2-product case solved by hand (a vertex of the feasible polygon), the units and the profit match within 1e-7 (HiGHS's default feasibility tolerance).
test_hints: Solve a two-product case by hand: list the vertices and their profits.

hints: A solution of a linear program satisfies its own constraints: recompute the resource use of the plan and compare it with the capacity.
behaviours.spec: The plan uses no resource beyond its capacity (within 1e-7) and no product has negative units.
test_hints: Recompute `use * units` and compare it with the capacity, with the solver's tolerance.

hints: A solver always hands back some numbers; whether they are an optimum is a separate question you must ask.
behaviours.spec: When the solver does not report an optimum (an unbounded plan, such as a product with a positive margin that uses no resource, or an infeasible one), `solve_plan` throws an `ErrorException`.
test_hints: Test a plan that has no optimum.

milestones.goal:
Model the plan as a linear program and solve it: one nonnegative variable
per product, one constraint per resource, and the total margin as the
objective to maximise. Turn the solver's log off (`set_silent`).

choices: HiGHS rounds whatever point it finds to the nearest vertex before it reports the solution, to remove noise
Along any edge the profit changes at a constant rate, so moving the better way pays until a constraint stops you
Points inside the feasible region break at least one constraint
A linear program has only one feasible point once all its constraints are written down, and that point is a vertex
questions.explain: A linear function has no interior maximum: from any point, moving in the direction that raises it keeps raising it at the same rate until a constraint becomes binding. Repeating that ends at a vertex (several vertices and the edge between them can tie).
misconceptions: HiGHS's simplex method moves from vertex to vertex; nothing is rounded. The vertex is where the optimum is, not an artefact.
Interior points satisfy every constraint with room to spare; they are feasible, just not optimal.
The feasible region is usually a polygon with infinitely many points; the vertices are its corners.
questions.prompt: The profit of a plan is linear in the units. Why is an optimal plan always found at a vertex of the feasible region (when there is an optimum)?

milestones.title: The linear program

api.doc: One per resource, in the order of the rows of `use`, nonnegative.

hints: A resource that is not used up is worth nothing extra; a binding one is worth the profit one more unit of it brings.
behaviours.spec: Each price equals the hand-computed dual within 1e-7 (HiGHS's dual feasibility tolerance), and (profit with capacity + delta) - profit, divided by delta, for a delta that keeps the same vertex; a resource with slack has price 0; there is one price per resource.
test_hints: Solve the dual of a small case by hand: the binding constraints give one equation per product made.

milestones.goal:
How much more profit would one more unit of each resource bring? Read the
dual values of the resource constraints and check them against a case you
solve by hand and by re-solving with a slightly larger capacity.

choices: Yes: each unit earns 1.5 in profit and costs only 1.2, so every one of the 12 units gains 0.3, which is 3.6 in all
No: the price holds only for 6 more units, after which resource 2 has slack; the deal gains 9 and costs 14.4
No: a shadow price is a cost, so each extra unit lowers the profit by 1.5
questions.explain: A shadow price is a derivative: it holds while the same constraints stay binding. Raising capacity 2 moves the vertex along 3x1 + 2x2 = 18 until x1 reaches 0 at capacity 18; beyond that resource 2 is slack and worth 0. Re-solving with capacity 24 gives profit 45, up 9 from 36.
misconceptions: That treats the price as constant for any amount. It is valid only while the current vertex stays optimal; past that the price can drop, here to 0.
A shadow price is the profit gained per extra unit, so it is nonnegative for a resource you can only have more of.
questions.prompt: In the plan max 3x1 + 5x2 with x1 <= 4, 2x2 <= 12, 3x1 + 2x2 <= 18, resource 2 has shadow price 1.5. A supplier offers 12 more units of it at 1.2 each. Is the deal worth it?

api.doc: The smallest margin of `product` at which it is made in the optimal plan, the other margins as given. `Inf` when it is not made at any margin up to 1e6.

hints: The units of the product, as a function of its margin, jump from 0 to positive at the break-even margin.
behaviours.spec: Within 1e-6 of the hand-computed value on a 2-product case (ten times HiGHS's dual feasibility tolerance), for `product = 1` and `product = 2`, whatever margin of that product is passed in.
test_hints: Work out a break-even margin by hand: with one resource, a product is made once its margin per unit of resource beats the other's.

hints: A bracket must contain the break-even margin, and that margin can be large.
behaviours.spec: The bracket is found, not fixed: break-even margins of 30 and 250 come out right (within 1e-6 relative).
test_hints: Test a break-even margin far above 10.

hints: Some products are never made at any margin: they need a resource there is none of.
behaviours.spec: A product that needs a resource with zero capacity is never made: the result is positive infinity (a `Float64`).
test_hints: Test a product that can never be made.

milestones.goal:
At what margin does a product start being made? As a function of its
margin m, the product's units in the optimal plan are 0 up to some margin
and positive beyond it. Find that margin with a bracketing method from
Roots.jl on units(m) - 1e-6 (the threshold sits above the solver's 1e-7
tolerance, so a product that is not made always gives a negative value).

choices: The function is a step: its slope is 0 wherever it exists
Newton's method needs the second derivative, which a linear program does not provide
Bisection always converges faster than Newton's method
questions.explain: units(m) is piecewise constant in m: it is 0 below the break-even margin and jumps there. Newton's method divides by the slope, which is 0 (or undefined at the jump), so it cannot move. Bisection uses only the sign, which does change across the jump.
misconceptions: Newton's method for a root needs the first derivative only; the problem is that this derivative is 0.
Newton's method converges faster (quadratically) on smooth functions; bisection is chosen here because it is the method that works on a jump.
questions.prompt: Why find the break-even margin by bisection rather than by Newton's method on units(m) - 1e-6?

milestones.title: Break-even margin

api.doc: argmax of (p - cost) q(p) for a demand function `q`, by LBFGS from `p0` with ForwardDiff gradients.
The same for q(p) = a exp(-b p).

hints: Set the derivative of (p - cost) a exp(-b p) to zero to get the price you expect.
behaviours.spec: `best_price(a, b, cost)` equals the closed form cost + 1/b within 1e-8 (Optim's gradient tolerance divided by the curvature at the optimum, on well-scaled cases).
test_hints: Derive the best price by hand and compare.

hints: The profit per unit sold is the price less the cost.
behaviours.spec: For other demand curves, such as q(p) = 10 - p, the result is the hand-computed argmax within 1e-8, and the start point `p0` is a keyword.
test_hints: Test a demand curve other than the exponential one.

hints: Optim can take a gradient you write, approximate one by finite differences, or ask an AD package.
behaviours.spec: The gradient comes from ForwardDiff, not from finite differences: during the search `q` is called with `ForwardDiff.Dual` numbers.
test_hints: Test what `q` is called with, not only the price.

milestones.goal:
Demand falls with price. For a demand curve q(p), choose the price that
maximises the margin times the demand, (p - cost) q(p), with Optim.jl's
LBFGS and exact gradients from ForwardDiff. In Optim 2 the keyword value
for that comes from `Optim.ADTypes` (unit 25 shows it); the older
`autodiff = :forward` of many tutorials is rejected with a `TypeError`.
Then the exponential curve q(p) = a exp(-b p), whose best price you can
derive by hand.

choices: LBFGS accepts only anonymous functions as its objective, so a named function with typed methods is rejected
ForwardDiff calls `q` with dual numbers, and the annotation allows only Float64
`exp` has no method for Float64 inside Optim
questions.explain: Forward-mode AD evaluates the objective on `ForwardDiff.Dual` numbers, which carry a value and a derivative. A method restricted to `Float64` has no method for them. Leave arguments untyped (or `::Real`) so the same function works on both.
misconceptions: Optim takes any callable; a named function works the same as an anonymous one when its methods accept the argument types.
`exp(::Float64)` exists everywhere; the call that fails is `q` itself, given a `Dual` its annotation does not allow.
questions.prompt: `best_price(p -> 100 * exp(-0.5p), 2.0)` works, but with `q(p::Float64) = 100 * exp(-0.5p)` it throws a `MethodError`. Why?

projects.name: production
projects.reading:
Prerequisites: course unit 25 (optimisation).

A product uses fixed amounts of each resource per unit and earns a fixed
margin; resources are limited per week. The plan is how many units of each
product to make. Throughout, `margin[p]` is the profit per unit of product
`p`, `use[r, p]` the amount of resource `r` one unit of product `p` needs
(all entries >= 0), and `capacity[r]` how much of resource `r` there is.

Solvers work to tolerances, so their answers are not exact. HiGHS's
defaults are 1e-7 for primal and dual feasibility; Optim's LBFGS stops when
the gradient is below 1e-8. Every `≈` in your tests needs an `atol` or
`rtol` and a one-line comment saying which of these it comes from. The
checker warns on `==` between floats inside `@test`.

This project's environment (`optim`) runs only in the container on Windows
hosts; `tutor guided check` uses it by default.

A Julia copy of a 1-D NumPy array; integer arrays are converted to Float64.

hints: Some conversions copy the data and others describe memory that already exists.
behaviours.spec: A write through the NumPy array returned by `as_numpy(v)` is visible in `v`, and a write to `v` is visible in the array.
test_hints: Change one side, read the other.

hints: A wrapper around Python memory changes when Python changes it.
behaviours.spec: `from_numpy(a)` is a `Vector{Float64}`; changing it does not change `a`, and changing `a` does not change it.
test_hints: Check the type, then change each side.

milestones.goal:
Two ways across the boundary, with the difference made testable: a view
shares the Julia vector's memory, a copy owns its own. Write through one side
and read the other to tell them apart.

choices:
3-element Vector{Float64}:
 7.0
 2.0
 3.0

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 7.0
 8.0
 3.0

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 1.0
 2.0
 3.0
questions.code:
using PythonCall
np = pyimport("numpy")
v = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
a = np.asarray(v)
b = np.array(v)
a[0] = 7.0
b[1] = 8.0
v
questions.explain: `np.asarray` reuses the Julia vector's memory, so writing `a[0]` changes `v[1]`. `np.array` copies by default, so `b` is separate and `v[2]` keeps its value.
misconceptions: `np.array` copies its input unless told otherwise (`copy=False`); only the `asarray` view shares `v`'s memory.
`np.asarray` makes no copy when its input already exposes a suitable buffer, and a Julia `Vector{Float64}` does.
questions.prompt: What does the last line show?

choices: The result must stay as it is whatever Python later does to `a`
A `PyArray` cannot be indexed, iterated or broadcast over from Julia code
Copying is faster than wrapping for arrays of any size
questions.explain: A `PyArray` is a view: it reads Python's memory, so a later write on the Python side shows through, and it is only valid while the Python object lives. A copy owns its data.
misconceptions: A `PyArray` is an `AbstractArray`: indexing, iteration and broadcasting all work on it.
Wrapping costs a few hundred bytes whatever the size; a copy costs 8 bytes per element. Milestone 4 measures this.
questions.prompt: Why does `from_numpy` return a new `Vector{Float64}` rather than `PyArray(a)`?

milestones.title: Copies and views

api.doc: A NumPy view of `A` (no copy) with `A[i, j] == a[i-1, j-1]` and shape `size(A)`.
For a 2-D array (in either memory order): a Julia copy with `M[i, j] == a[i-1, j-1]`.

hints: A square matrix can hide swapped indices; use a non-square one.
behaviours.spec: For a non-square `A`, `as_numpy(A)` has shape `size(A)` and element `(i-1, j-1)` equal to `A[i, j]`.
test_hints: Use a 2 × 3 matrix with distinct entries.

hints: Making the array C-ordered means copying it into a new layout.
behaviours.spec: `as_numpy(A)` shares memory with `A` (a write through it changes `A`) and NumPy reports it as Fortran-ordered (`a.flags.f_contiguous`).
test_hints: Write through the view and read the matrix.

hints: Arrays made by NumPy are row-major; reading their flat buffer column by column scrambles a non-square matrix.
behaviours.spec: `from_numpy` on a C-ordered (row-major) 2-D array returns a `Matrix{Float64}` with `M[i, j] == a[i-1, j-1]`.
test_hints: Make the array on the NumPy side, so it is row-major.

milestones.goal:
Matrices: Julia stores a matrix column by column, NumPy defaults to row by
row. The bytes can be shared if NumPy is told how to read them (its strides).
Make indices mean the same thing on both sides, in both directions.

choices: `a.flags.f_contiguous` is true: the same bytes, read column by column
`a.flags.c_contiguous` is true: NumPy copied it into row-major order
`a.shape` is (3, 2): NumPy reads Julia's column-major bytes as rows instead
questions.explain: Julia exposes the matrix's memory with its strides (8 bytes down a column, 16 across a row). NumPy keeps those strides, so the view is Fortran-ordered, shape (2, 3), and no data moved.
misconceptions: `np.asarray` copies only when it must; a Julia matrix already describes its layout, so NumPy uses it as it is.
The shape comes with the strides: NumPy reads the bytes in Julia's order, so `a[i-1, j-1]` is `A[i, j]` and the shape is (2, 3).
questions.prompt: A 2 × 3 Julia matrix `A` goes to NumPy as `a = np.asarray(A)`. What does NumPy report?

api.doc: Via `numpy.convolve` on the valid part only.
In Julia: a running sum, one result vector, nothing allocated per window.

hints: Work out a window of 2 over four values by hand and compare.
behaviours.spec: `moving_average(v, k)` has length n - k + 1 and entry i equal to the mean of `v[i:i+k-1]`.
test_hints: Compare with means you work out by hand.

hints: A convolution with a kernel of k equal weights is a moving average, if the weights are right and only full windows are kept.
behaviours.spec: `moving_average_np(v, k)` gives the same n - k + 1 means, computed by `numpy.convolve`.
test_hints: Check the length as well as the values.

hints: The two add in different orders, so they round differently; the question is by how much.
behaviours.spec: On 10^5 random values both return `Vector{Float64}` and agree within (n + k) · eps · max|v|: the running sum makes n updates, each rounding by at most eps times a partial sum of size k · max|v|, and the result is divided by k.
test_hints: Test on large random data, not only on small exact cases.

hints: A window of 0 values has no mean.
behaviours.spec: Both throw an `ArgumentError` when k is not in 1:n.
test_hints: Test the calls that should fail.

milestones.goal:
A moving average with window k: the mean of each of the n - k + 1 full
windows. Write it twice, in NumPy (`np.convolve`) and in Julia with a running
sum (add the value entering the window, subtract the one leaving), and test
that they agree to a tolerance you derive.

The Julia version is also graded for performance against the reference: same
speed class, no allocation per window, linear growth in n, type-stable.

choices: Nothing is wrong: summing in another order rounds differently, well within the bound
The running sum has a bug: exact arithmetic gives equal results, so floating point must too
NumPy computes in single precision unless the dtype is passed explicitly
questions.explain: The bound (n + k) · eps · max|v| is about 2e-9 here. Each method rounds at different points, so a difference of 1e-12 is expected and far inside it.
misconceptions: Floating-point addition is not associative: the same sum in another order gives another rounding, so equal results are not expected.
`np.ones(k)` and an array from a `Vector{Float64}` are float64, so the convolution is in double precision.
questions.prompt: On 10^5 values near 100 with k = 50, the running sum and `np.convolve` differ by about 1e-12. What does that tell you?

api.doc: `@allocated` of `as_numpy` (view) and of `from_numpy` (copy) on a vector of length n, after a warm-up call of each.

hints: A view is a small Python object pointing at memory that already exists.
behaviours.spec: `boundary_bytes(n).view` is under 10 KiB for n = 10 and for n = 10^6 (it does not grow with n).
test_hints: Measure at two very different sizes.

hints: A copy of n Float64 values needs 8n bytes for the data alone.
behaviours.spec: `boundary_bytes(n).copy` is at least 8n bytes at n = 10^6, and doubling n adds about 8n bytes (within 1%).
test_hints: Check the size, and how it grows.

milestones.goal:
Measure, do not assume: how many bytes does each conversion allocate? A view
should cost a small constant (the Python object), a copy 8 bytes per element
plus a constant. Measure the second call of each: the first one compiles.

choices: The first call also counts memory used to compile the method
The garbage collector frees the first call's memory late
PythonCall caches the NumPy array after the first call
questions.explain: `@allocated` counts every allocation during the call, including the compiler's work the first time a method runs for these argument types. The second call shows what the conversion itself costs.
misconceptions: `@allocated` counts bytes allocated, not bytes still alive, so when the collector runs does not change it.
Each call makes a new NumPy array object; nothing is cached between calls, which is why the second call still allocates.
questions.prompt: `@allocated as_numpy(v)` reports 1416 bytes on its first call and 744 on its second. Why does the spec measure the second?

api.doc: A new table with the columns of `df` plus a Bool column `valid`; `df` itself is not changed.

behaviours.spec: Site names have surrounding spaces removed and are lower-case (`" North "` becomes `"north"`).
test_hints: Give `clean` a site name that differs from the cleaned one in more than one way.

hints: Every temperature in the result should be in the same unit, and the `unit` column should say so.
behaviours.spec: Rows with unit `F` have their temperature converted to Celsius and their unit set to `C`; Celsius rows and missing temperatures are unchanged.
test_hints: Test a Fahrenheit value whose Celsius value you know exactly.

hints: Look at rows 3 and 4 of data/readings.csv.
behaviours.spec: Rows that are equal after the cleaning above are removed, keeping the first one, in the original order.
test_hints: Put an exact duplicate in your test table and count the rows after cleaning.

hints: The rule has three parts; check each against the spec separately.
behaviours.spec: `valid` is false when the temperature is missing or outside -50 to 60 °C, or the humidity is outside 0 to 100 %; a missing humidity alone does not make a row invalid. The bounds themselves are valid. No row is dropped.
test_hints: Test a valid row, an invalid row, and a row on each bound.

hints: A function without `!` in its name should leave its arguments alone.
behaviours.spec: The `DataFrame` passed in is the same after the call as before it.
test_hints: Keep a copy of the input, call `clean`, and compare.

milestones.goal:
Turn the table from milestone 1 into one you can trust: one spelling per
site, one temperature unit, no repeated rows, and a flag for readings
that cannot be right. Flag them, do not drop them: someone may want to
know how many readings each sensor got wrong.

choices: Bad rows are evidence about the sensors, which a later step may need
Deleting rows from a DataFrame copies every column, which is slow for big files
A DataFrame cannot have rows removed once it has been created
questions.explain: Cleaning should not destroy information that a later step may need; `summarize` filters on `valid`, and anyone can still ask which sensor misbehaved.
misconceptions: Filtering is a single pass over the columns; speed is not the reason.
`deleteat!`, `filter!` and indexing remove rows; the choice here is about keeping information.
questions.prompt: Why flag invalid readings in a `valid` column instead of deleting those rows in `clean`?

milestones.title: Cleaning without losing information

api.doc: Input: the output of `clean`. Output columns: site, date (a `Date`), n, mean_temp, max_temp, mean_humidity.

hints: The summary should not see readings the cleaning step flagged.
behaviours.spec: Only rows with `valid == true` are counted and averaged.
test_hints: Include an invalid row with an extreme temperature in your test table.

hints: `time` holds a date and a clock time; the summary is per day.
behaviours.spec: Groups are (site, calendar day); `date` is a `Date` column.
test_hints: Use two days for one site in your test.

hints: `mean` of a vector that contains `missing` is `missing`.
behaviours.spec: `mean_humidity` is the mean of the humidity values present in the group, and `missing` when the group has none.
test_hints: Put one missing humidity in a group that has other humidity values.

hints: The order of groups follows the order they appear in unless you ask for another.
behaviours.spec: Rows are sorted by site, then by date.
test_hints: Put the sites in your test table out of alphabetical order.

milestones.goal:
Summarise a cleaned table: one row per site and calendar day, over the
valid readings only.

choices: `mean` propagates `missing`: one missing value makes the sum missing
`groupby` drops missing values before `combine` sees them
`combine` converts missing values to zero
questions.explain: Missing values propagate through arithmetic by design, so a mean is never silently computed over fewer values than you think; `skipmissing` makes skipping them explicit.
misconceptions: `groupby` keeps every row; the groups are made from the key columns, not the values.
Nothing in DataFrames turns missing into zero for you; that would bias the mean.
questions.prompt: `combine(groupby(v, [:site, :date]), :humidity => mean => :mean_humidity)` gives `missing` for a day where one humidity reading is missing. Why?

milestones.title: Split, apply, combine

api.doc: A header line; dates as yyyy-mm-dd; mean_temp, max_temp and mean_humidity rounded to 2 decimals; NA for missing.
Read what write_summary wrote: site::String, date::Date, n::Int, the three numbers as Float64 (or with missing).

hints: By default CSV.jl writes nothing at all for a missing value.
behaviours.spec: A missing value is written as `NA`.
test_hints: Write a summary with a missing humidity and look at the text.

hints: A mean like 20.333333333333332 is noise in a report.
behaviours.spec: The three numeric summary columns are rounded to 2 decimals in the file (the table passed in is not changed).
test_hints: Use a value with more than two decimals in your test summary.

hints: Reading has the same pitfalls as milestone 1.
behaviours.spec: `read_summary(io)` of what `write_summary` wrote gives the same column names, `String` sites, `Date` dates and the rounded numbers, with `missing` where `NA` was written.
test_hints: Write, read back, and compare the tables.

milestones.goal:
Write a summary as CSV for people and other programs, and read such a file
back into a table with the same columns and types.
milestones.title: Writing it back

projects.reading:
Prerequisites: course unit 21 (DataFrames and CSV) and unit 12 (modules).
`data/readings.csv` is the file this project is about; open it and look at
it before you start. Every function you write takes and returns plain
values (an `IO`, a `DataFrame`), so you can test it with small tables you
build in the test itself.
projects.summary: Build a small package that reads a CSV of temperature and humidity readings with three kinds of missing marker, mixed units and inconsistent site names, cleans it without losing information, summarises it per site and day with split-apply-combine, and writes the summary back out so it reads in again unchanged. You write the code and the tests.
projects.title: Tidy: clean and summarise a messy sensor CSV
